Retrieval-augmented generation offers several concrete advantages over
letting a language model answer purely from what it memorized during
training. The most cited benefit is reduced hallucination: grounding an
answer in retrieved evidence lowers the rate of fabricated claims, because
the model has real text to draw from instead of only its own parametric
memory. Closely related is source grounding — because the retrieved
passages are known, an answer can cite exactly which document it came
from, which lets a reader verify the claim instead of trusting it blindly.

RAG also keeps a system's knowledge up to date without retraining the
underlying model. When the underlying documents change, re-indexing the
corpus is enough to refresh what the system knows; there is no need to
fine-tune or retrain the language model itself. This makes RAG a far more
cost-effective way to adapt a language model to a new knowledge domain
than fine-tuning a separate model per domain would be.

Domain customization follows from the same property: a private or
proprietary corpus can be plugged into the retriever without ever exposing
that data to the model during training, which matters for organizations
that cannot send sensitive documents to a third-party training pipeline.
Finally, retrieval improves recall on long-tail facts — rare, specific
details that a general-purpose parametric model was never trained heavily
on, or has since forgotten, can still be found and surfaced as long as
they exist somewhere in the indexed corpus.
